title: Signature Camp Hero Station Redesign
body:
A Signature redesign of a coastal radar station keeps the documented job, watching the sea approaches, and rebuilds the station as a compact Signature post with a single tower, a small crew building, and a public trail that passes the tower at a viewing distance.

Signature design. The design places the tower on the highest stable ground, the crew building behind a windbreak, and the trail on already disturbed ground so that visitors see the tower without entering any working area. Power comes from a shore connection with a small backup unit, and every building carries a visible label stating its job, so that no visitor has to guess what a structure is for. The tower's antenna is drawn as a rotating panel whose sweep is marked on a ground diagram at the trail viewpoint.

Use and limits. Use this design as a template for any coastal watch post that must be both working and publicly legible. Do not use it as a description of the real Camp Hero, because the real station's layout and history are covered in the public edition.

Design detail. The redesign is drawn in three layers so that each layer can be checked on its own: the tower layer shows the antenna, its rotation, and its sweep; the crew layer shows the building, its windbreak, and its power connection; and the public layer shows the trail, the viewpoint, and the fence line. A reviewer checks the tower layer for a clear sweep with no blind sector toward the sea, the crew layer for a power route that does not cross the trail, and the public layer for a viewpoint that gives a full view of the tower without letting a visitor reach it. If any layer fails its check, only that layer is redrawn, which keeps the redesign honest about what is working and what still needs work.

title: Signature Long-Range Watch Panel
body:
A Signature long-range watch panel replaces a room of scopes with one panel that shows contacts as labeled marks on a coastal chart, with range rings drawn from the tower's position.

Signature design. The panel draws range rings at fixed distances, plots each contact with its bearing and range, and colors a contact by its identification state: known traffic, unknown track, or clutter. Operators confirm an unknown track by checking it against the day's flight list before escalating, and the panel logs every confirmation with a time stamp. The demo plots three contacts and prints their identification states.

Use and limits. Use this design for teaching how radar watch duty works without needing real radar data. Do not use it as a working air defense system, because it is a teaching design fed by invented example contacts.

Design detail. The panel's identification states are deliberately few, because a watch operator under time pressure needs three clear choices rather than a dozen ambiguous ones. Known traffic is checked against the day's flight list and then set aside, clutter is marked and ignored unless it moves against the wind or the sea state in a way that suggests a real contact, and unknown tracks stay highlighted until an operator confirms or dismisses them with a reason. Every dismissal is logged with the operator's reason, so that a later reviewer can see whether unknowns were dismissed for good reasons or merely to clear the screen.

title: Signature Station-to-Park Conversion Kit
body:
A Signature kit for converting a closed station into a park lists every building, marks each one keep, secure, or remove, and lays trails before any building is opened to the public.

Signature design. The kit works in four passes: survey, hazard marking, trail layout, and sign installation. Each building gets a card with its condition, its hazards, and its decision, and no trail is opened until every building beside it has a decision. Signs state the building's former job in plain words and the reason for its present state, so visitors learn the history without entering anything.

Use and limits. Use this kit as a planning checklist for any former military site becoming public land. Do not use it as a substitute for professional hazard assessment, because real buildings need real surveyors.

Design detail. The kit's four passes are ordered so that no public use begins before safety is settled. The survey pass photographs and measures every building, the hazard pass marks structural, chemical, and electrical risks in plain words, the trail pass routes paths only past buildings that have decisions, and the sign pass writes the history of each building in one short paragraph. A building marked remove is fenced until removal, a building marked secure is locked and inspected on a schedule, and a building marked keep as ruin is stabilized so that it cannot collapse onto a trail. The kit's cards are kept as the park's own record.

title: Signature Lighthouse Keeper's Log
body:
A Signature keeper's log for a point lighthouse records each night's lamp state, weather, and passing traffic in a single line per night, so that a year's watch fits in a small book.

Signature design. Each line carries a date, a lamp code, a weather word, and a count of vessels seen, and the log's weekly summary counts nights the lamp burned clean against nights it needed attention. The demo writes seven example nights and prints the clean-burn count, showing how a simple log turns nightly work into a readable record.

Use and limits. Use this log design for any small station that needs a durable paper record. Do not use it as a historical document, because its entries are invented examples.

Design detail. The log's weekly summary is its most useful feature, because a week of single lines becomes a pattern: a lamp that needs attention twice in one week is inspected, a lamp that burns clean all week is left alone, and a vessel count that spikes on one night is noted for the harbor record. The log uses fixed codes so that any keeper can read any other keeper's entries, and it leaves a blank line after each week for notes about storms, repairs, and visitors. Over a year, the book becomes a small history of the point's weather and traffic, written by the people who watched it.

title: Signature Legend-Checking Worksheet
body:
A Signature worksheet for checking a legend gives every claim four boxes: earliest telling, records it should have left, physical traces it should show, and later additions, and a claim passes only when all four boxes hold evidence.

Signature design. The worksheet is used claim by claim, not story by story, so that a legend with ten claims gets ten verdicts instead of one blanket judgment. Each box is filled with a source or marked empty, and an empty box is itself a finding: it means the claim is unsupported at that check. The demo runs the worksheet over three example claims and prints how many boxes each one fills.

Use and limits. Use this worksheet for any contested story, from local legends to product claims. Do not use it to declare a claim false merely because one box is empty, because absence of evidence is a verdict of unverified, not of disproven.

Design detail. The worksheet's four boxes are filled in order, and the order matters. The earliest telling box prevents a late retelling from posing as an original source, the records box prevents a story from surviving on testimony alone when documents should exist, the physical traces box prevents a story from ignoring what the site itself shows, and the later additions box prevents growth from posing as corroboration. A claim that fills only the testimony box is marked as a story awaiting evidence, which is a fair verdict that neither endorses nor insults the people who told it, and a claim that fills all four boxes is marked as supported pending further checking.

title: Signature Magnetic Signature Reducer
body:
A Signature magnetic signature reducer is a teaching model of degaussing: a hull model carries a field value, coils carry a cancelling value, and the sum shows the reduced signature.

Signature design. The model starts with a hull field, adds coil currents in steps, and prints the remaining field after each step, so a student can see that cancellation is partial and that stronger coils reduce the field further but never to zero in practice. The demo runs three coil settings and prints the remaining field for each.

Use and limits. Use this model to teach why degaussing helps against magnetic mines without making a ship invisible. Do not use it as naval engineering, because real degaussing needs real hull measurements.

Design detail. The teaching model shows three lessons that real degaussing also teaches. First, cancellation is partial: coils reduce a field but do not erase it, so a ship is quieter rather than silent. Second, stronger coils help only up to a point, because the power and weight of the coils grow while the remaining field shrinks more slowly. Third, the field changes with heading and with the earth's field where the ship sails, so a setting that works in one place needs adjustment in another. Students who run the model with different coil settings learn all three lessons from the numbers rather than from a lecture.

title: Signature Book-Series Growth Map
body:
A Signature growth map tracks how a book series adds claims over time: each book is a row, each claim a column, and a mark shows which book first made which claim.

Signature design. The map makes retelling growth visible: claims that appear only in later books, with no earlier source, stand out as additions rather than as original testimony. The demo builds a small map of three books and four claims and prints which claims are first-book claims and which are later additions.

Use and limits. Use this map for any series where later volumes expand an original story. Do not use it as proof about any particular book, because its example claims are invented for teaching.

Design detail. The growth map's value appears when a series is long, because a reader of the tenth book cannot remember which claims the first book made. The map restores that memory in one view: first-book claims sit in the first column, and every later addition is dated to the book that introduced it. A claim that appears in book five with no earlier source is then visible as a fifth-book claim, and a reader can ask what evidence book five offered for it. The map does not judge whether a later claim is true; it only shows when the claim entered the story, which is the fact most often lost in retelling.

title: Signature Program Separation Chart
body:
A Signature separation chart keeps two real programs apart: each program gets its own column with its own dates, places, and documented actions, and any claim linking them must cite a document in both columns.

Signature design. The chart's rule is simple: a link claim without a document in each column is marked unlinked, and unlinked claims are never drawn as connections. The demo charts two example programs and prints the link verdict for a claim that tries to join them.

Use and limits. Use this chart whenever two famous programs are merged in a story. Do not use it as a historical finding about any real program, because its example rows are teaching material.

Design detail. The separation chart's rule about documents in both columns exists because merged stories usually cite documents from only one program and then treat the merger as proven. A chart that forces a document from each side makes the merger earn its connection: a laboratory report from one program and a radar log from the other, dated to the same period and naming the same place, would be a real link, while a report from one side alone is only half a link. The chart also keeps a list of claims that were checked and found unlinked, so that the same merger cannot be proposed again as if it had never been examined.

title: Signature Fiction-Inspiration Tracker
body:
A Signature tracker for fiction inspirations records a show's working title, its finished setting, and the point at which the setting changed, so that inspiration is never mistaken for documentation.

Signature design. The tracker has three fields per show: early setting, finished setting, and change note, and it prints a one-line summary stating the connection type. The demo tracks one example show from a coastal working title to a fictional inland town and prints the summary.

Use and limits. Use this tracker for any show said to be based on a real place. Do not use it as a production history of any real show, because its example row is invented.

Design detail. The tracker's change note is its most important field, because a setting change is where inspiration most often gets mistaken for documentation. When a show moves from a real coastal town to a fictional inland town, everything after the move belongs to fiction, and only the mood and the starting idea belong to the real place. The tracker therefore records the move explicitly, with the date or production stage at which it happened, and its one-line summary always states the connection type in plain words. A reader who sees inspiration, not documentation, will not go looking for fictional events at a real address.

title: Signature Beach Find Identifier
body:
A Signature beach find identifier compares an unknown carcass against local species by size, teeth, and fur, and ranks decomposition effects before ranking exotic explanations.

Signature design. The identifier lists candidate species, scores each against the observed features, and applies a decomposition adjustment that explains bloating and fur loss before any unusual candidate is considered. The demo scores two candidates for an example find and prints the better fit.

Use and limits. Use this identifier as a teaching tool for wildlife identification. Do not use it as a veterinary verdict, because real finds need real specimens and experts.

Design detail. The identifier's decomposition adjustment is applied before any exotic candidate is scored, because water changes a carcass in predictable ways that mimic strangeness. Bloating rounds the body, fur loss exposes skin and teeth, and the loss of soft tissue around the snout can make a familiar muzzle look beaked. The identifier lists these effects beside the observed features, so that a scorer can see which oddities decomposition already explains and which, if any, remain unexplained. Only features that survive the adjustment are scored against exotic candidates, which keeps the identifier from inventing monsters out of ordinary decay.

title: Signature Warning Network Model
body:
A Signature warning network model links four nodes, two radars, one control center, and one interceptor base, and shows how a contact report travels from detection to decision.

Signature design. Each node adds a time cost, and the model prints the total warning time for a contact, showing why communications matter as much as radar range. The demo runs one contact through the chain and prints each leg's time and the total.

Use and limits. Use this model to teach network thinking about defense systems. Do not use it as a working defense design, because its times are teaching values.

Design detail. The network model's lesson is that warning time is a chain, and a chain is only as fast as its slowest leg. A radar that detects instantly is wasted if its report waits for a slow communication link, and a fast link is wasted if correlation takes minutes to decide that two reports describe one aircraft. The model therefore prints each leg separately, so that a student can see where time is lost and can test improvements leg by leg: faster reporting, faster correlation, or faster orders. The total at the end is the only number that matters to the defended area, because an aircraft is intercepted on the total, not on any single leg.

title: Signature Source Criticism Ladder
body:
A Signature source criticism ladder ranks evidence from strongest to weakest: contemporary documents, physical traces, contemporary photographs, later testimony, and retellings, and a claim must cite the highest available rung.

Signature design. The ladder is used by placing each source on its rung and then reading the claim's support from the top down: if only the bottom rungs hold sources, the claim is marked weakly supported. The demo ranks five example sources and prints the claim's verdict.

Use and limits. Use this ladder for any historical claim. Do not use it as a substitute for archival research, because ranking sources is only the first step of checking them.

Design detail. The ladder's rungs are ordered by how close a source stands to the event it describes. Contemporary documents stand highest because they were written when the event happened and for purposes other than telling the story, physical traces stand next because they cannot be misremembered, contemporary photographs stand next because they show but do not explain, later testimony stands lower because memory changes, and retellings stand lowest because they repeat rather than witness. A claim supported only from the bottom rungs is not necessarily false, but it is weakly supported, and the ladder's verdict says exactly that, no more and no less.

title: Signature Park Visit Planner
body:
A Signature park visit planner takes a trail list with distances and viewpoints and builds a route that stays on marked trails, passes the tower viewpoint, and returns before dark.

Signature design. The planner sums trail distances, checks the total against the visitor's available hours, and prints the route with its viewpoints in order. The demo plans a route of three trails and prints the total distance and the viewpoints.

Use and limits. Use this planner as a template for park route tools. Do not use it as a map of any real park, because its trails are invented examples.

Design detail. The planner's route rule is that a route must return before dark, which is why it sums distances before it lists viewpoints. A route that passes every viewpoint but strands a visitor after sunset is a failed route, and the planner rejects it rather than printing it. The planner also orders viewpoints by the trail rather than by fame, so that a visitor follows the ground instead of backtracking, and it marks any viewpoint beside a closed building with a viewing-only note. A planned route is therefore a promise the planner can keep: marked trails, real distances, and a return time.

title: Signature Claim Table Builder
body:
A Signature claim table builder takes a list of claims and prints a four-column table: claim, evidence needed, evidence offered, and verdict, with unverified as the default verdict.

Signature design. The builder never upgrades a verdict without a source: a claim with testimony only stays unverified, and only a claim with a document or a physical trace moves to supported. The demo builds a table for three example claims and prints their verdicts.

Use and limits. Use this builder for any contested topic. Do not use it as a verdict on any real claim, because its example claims are teaching material.

Design detail. The claim table's default verdict of unverified is a discipline, not a judgment. A new claim starts unverified because no evidence has been entered for it yet, and it moves only when a source is entered in the evidence column. Testimony moves a claim to weakly supported at most, because testimony alone cannot carry a claim about physical events, while a document or a physical trace can move it to supported. The table keeps every claim's history, so that a claim once marked supported can be returned to unverified if its source is later shown to be unreliable, and the table never deletes a claim to hide a change of verdict.

title: Signature Harbor Year Planner
body:
A Signature harbor year planner divides a fishing town's year into seasons, assigns each season its main catch and its main work, and prints the year's rhythm in one table.

Signature design. The planner's value is balance: it shows that a harbor town's life is a cycle of seasons rather than a single event, and it gives each season equal weight. The demo prints four seasons with their catches and work.

Use and limits. Use this planner as a template for seasonal town profiles. Do not use it as a history of any real harbor, because its seasons are teaching examples.

Design detail. The harbor planner's four seasons are given equal weight on purpose, because a harbor town's year is not one season of work and three seasons of waiting. Spring repair decides whether summer boats run, summer trips pay for winter maintenance, fall processing turns the catch into income that lasts, and winter mending keeps skills alive when the water is rough. A planner that showed only the busy season would mislead a newcomer about what harbor life costs and what it returns, while the full year shows a cycle that has supported the town for generations and that any new harbor project must respect.

title: Signature Layered Interpretation Sign
body:
A Signature layered interpretation sign presents one site in three labeled bands: documented history, present-day park, and legend, with the legend band marked as story in its heading.

Signature design. The sign's rule is that no band borrows another band's authority: the legend band never cites the history band, and the history band never cites the legend band. The demo prints a sign for an example site with its three bands and their labels.

Use and limits. Use this sign design for any contested heritage site. Do not use it as a sign for any real site, because its example text is invented.

Design detail. The layered sign's bands are separated by color and by heading so that a visitor cannot mistake one band for another even at a glance. The history band uses a plain heading and past-tense verbs, the park band uses present-tense verbs and directions, and the legend band uses a heading that contains the word story, so that every sentence in it is read as story. The sign's rule about borrowing authority is enforced by its writers: a legend sentence may not cite a history document, and a history sentence may not cite a legend book, and any draft that breaks the rule is rewritten before the sign is made.
